title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Using Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators combined with a logical-OR decision rule, and a matched sample of N = 300 intents (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants), we compared single-pass LLM generation (baseline) to an LLM+verifier GVR pipeline under a frozen protocol (preregistration cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). The run used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM candidate generated per pair and replayed to both arms) and consumed model_calls_used = 300. Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (paired contingency n11 = 300; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). McNemar two-sided p = 1.0, paired risk-difference = 0.0, bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). No validator detected forbidden reachability and no repair calls were invoked; observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. Because the repair path was never exercised, the experiment demonstrates that inserting a verifier does not change observed compliance when baseline generation already satisfies the safety predicate under the chosen contract; it does not provide evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations. We summarize design lessons (generation semantics, adversary potency, verifier diversity, and repair budgeting) and point readers to archived execution and analysis artifacts that substantiate all reported numbers.

sections.introduction: LLMs can automate intent-driven network configuration but introduce operational risks: generated artifacts may expand attack surface, violate access control, or otherwise produce security-relevant regressions. Prior system and survey work therefore emphasizes execution oracles, constrained generation, and iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as operational mitigations. Motivated by an evidence gap—preregistered, deterministic, paired evaluations that quantify whether an in-loop verifier reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations under adversarial inputs—we designed and executed a confirmatory paired study. The research question is: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? Our contributions are (1) a preregistered paired confirmatory design (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) and deterministic execution with archived artifacts, (2) a concise, artifact-grounded report of the completed run and its degenerate confirmatory outcome (n11 = 300), (3) numeric uncertainty bounds (McNemar p, bootstrap CI, Clopper–Pearson upper bound) derived from the archived per-episode outcomes, and (4) practical design lessons and reproducibility pointers to guide follow-up stress tests aimed at exercising the repair path.
sections.related_work: Generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures have improved correctness for code and IaC tasks by using verifier feedback to guide repairs; system papers show verifier power and repair strategy substantially affect realized gains. Surveys and NetOps studies document LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and commonly recommend integrating validators, constrained generation, or human oversight. Emulation and testbed work demonstrates that execution-based validation is feasible for research-grade evaluation but cautions that external validity to production devices and live traffic remains an open concern. Our study sits at the intersection of these strands by providing a preregistered, paired, deterministic evaluation that focuses squarely on the operationally meaningful security predicate—forbidden reachability—and archives per-episode validator traces to enable auditability.
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration: We preregistered a paired binary design with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds and 150 programmatic adversarial variants). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in proportion of intents yielding forbidden reachability). The confirmatory test is an exact McNemar two-sided test (alpha = 0.05). Prespecified CI method: bootstrap percentile; final analysis used 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729) as recorded in the analysis log. Sampling and contamination checks (exact duplicates and fuzzy deduplication at normalized edit-distance < 0.15) were performed deterministically per preregistration.

Forbidden-reachability predicate and validators (concise technical definition): The forbidden-reachability predicate flags configurations that create any new source→destination forwarding connectivity that the task's security policy labels as disallowed (policy-specified forbidden pairs and protected interfaces). For this study the policy class includes intent-level protected_interfaces and workflow constraints encoded in each task (e.g., mgmt1 as a protected interface); predicates consider routing and ACL/route-policy semantics as modeled by the validators. Two deterministic validators were used: (1) a containerized execution validator (Batfish-style) that applies the generated configuration inside the Dockerized emulator and observes forwarding/connectivity and configured ACL/route-policy effects via deterministic packet-reachability checks; and (2) a lightweight Python static reachability analyzer that builds a graph model from normalized configuration commands and evaluates reachability via static inference rules. Validator outputs include structured validator_trace fields (validation_before/after, violation_codes, validation.valid) archived per episode. Validators were combined with a logical-OR decision rule: a pair is labeled 'violating' if any validator reports forbidden reachability. Known limitations: execution validators depend on emulator fidelity (control-plane convergence and device model effects), and static analyzers may underapproximate dynamic forwarding behaviors (ECMP, stateful devices); both classes can produce false negatives under semantics not modeled by the validator.

Adapter contract, generation semantics, and repair policy: To limit provider usage we preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each paired intent one initial LLM candidate is generated and replayed to both arms (baseline = replay, guarded = validate and, if forbidden reachability is detected, allow up to one repair LLM call). This contract yields exactly one hosted-model call per pair (model_calls_used = 300) instead of two independent draws per pair (up to 600). Repair calls are only invoked if a validator-detected forbidden-reachability predicate fires; repair attempt logic, prompt templates, and maximum attempts (one repair per pair) were preregistered and archived. All sampling seeds, task payloads, emulator composition, and deterministic orchestration are recorded in the execution task manifest for replay.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting summary: Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 arms); completed = 600; failed = 0. Provider-call accounting under shared_initial_candidate semantics: model_calls_used = 300 (stage_counts: 'shared_initial_generation' = 300). Representative archived artifacts substantiate these counts (see Verification paragraph below).

Primary confirmatory statistics (compact): Paired contingency (guarded vs baseline): n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Observing 0 violations in 300 independent episodes gives a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the baseline violation probability ≈ 0.00994 (≈0.994%).

Repair activity and verifier concordance: No validator reported forbidden reachability on any initial candidate, therefore no repair call was invoked (all per-episode validator_trace.repair_applied = false). The two validators were concordant across episodes (verifier_disagreement_rate = 0 in archived summaries). Because no discordant pairs occurred, the McNemar test is uninformative about repair efficacy: without discordant outcomes there is no evidence that repair could have changed an initial violating outcome into a nonviolating one.

Representative examples: Typical medium- and hard-difficulty tasks (shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) appear in the archived representative tasks; per-episode scoring artifacts show normalized configurations, parsed command counts, and validation.valid = true for both baseline and guarded arms in the examples. All per-episode raw responses, validator_trace entries, and the paired contingency table are archived and consistent with the numeric summary above.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and limits of what the evidence shows: Under the exact adapter contract (shared_initial_candidate), declared model (gpt-5-mini), two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, emulator, and the programmatic adversarial variants used here, baseline generation satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate for all sampled intents; thus inserting the verifier did not change observed compliance. The results are internally consistent: provider-call accounting, per-episode validator traces, and the paired contingency are mutually coherent in the archived artifacts.

What the evidence does not show: Because the repair path was never exercised, the experiment provides no evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue violating initial candidates. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and a target 30 percentage-point absolute reduction; the observed degenerate contingency violates that assumption and renders the planned confirmatory test moot for repair efficacy. Researchers should therefore not interpret the null paired difference as evidence that verifiers are unnecessary across deployments.

Design lessons grounded in the run: (1) Generation semantics matter: shared_initial_candidate reduces model-call cost (here model_calls_used = 300) but also reduces independent-sample variance needed to produce discordant violations; independent-condition generation (two draws per pair) or larger sample sizes better exercise repair efficacy at increased provider cost. (2) Adversary potency matters: the deterministic adversarial variants used here did not trigger validator-detectable forbidden reachability for the chosen model and validators—stronger or targeted adversaries are needed to stress repair paths. (3) Verifier diversity and strength matter: combining multiple verifier families and improving emulator fidelity increases the chance of detecting realistic violations but raises reproducibility and cost trade-offs. (4) Reproducibility is practical: archived per-episode raw responses, validator traces, provider-call audit, and the analysis log permit exact replication of the reported accounting and contingency outcomes.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation (declared LLM: gpt-5-mini) with two deterministic validators and shared_initial_candidate semantics. The run completed N = 300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 and produced a degenerate outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never reported violations, no repair calls were executed and the experiment cannot evaluate whether verifier-guided repair rescues violating outputs. The main practical contribution is deterministic execution accounting, artifact archiving, and concrete design lessons (generation semantics, adversary strength, verifier diversity, repair budgeting) to inform follow-up stress tests intended to exercise repair paths (for example: independent-condition generation, stronger targeted adversaries, multi-model comparisons, and more diverse oracles). All principal numeric claims and per-episode traces are archived to support independent verification and reanalysis.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: validators never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: programmatic generation produced one adversarial variant per benign seed; archived generation seeds and intent payloads are available in execution/task_manifest.jsonl for reproducibility, but these perturbations did not trigger validator-detectable forbidden reachability for the tested model/validators.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.

Model and verifier scope: a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
